articles.title: Groq in 2026: How Fast It Really Is, and When Speed Isn't Worth It
articles.excerpt: Is Groq Worth It for Solo Devs Chasing Low Latency in 2026? Latency is the feature nobody puts on the roadmap and everybody notices, and it decides whether users stay with an interface or quietly aban…
articles.body: Is Groq Worth It for Solo Devs Chasing Low Latency in 2026? Latency is the feature nobody puts on the roadmap and everybody notices, and it decides whether users stay with an interface or quietly abandon it. A chat interface that starts answering in under a second feels like a different product from one that starts after three, and if you are building voice, autocomplete, or an agent that makes several model calls in sequence, per-call delay compounds into something users abandon. Groq is the provider most often recommended for that problem. Here is an honest look at where it earns its place, where it is the wrong tool, and what to check before you commit.
articles.author: guang diyuzhi

articles.title: Zero-Trust Sandboxing for AI Agents: Why Process Isolation Alone Won't Stop Prompt Injection
articles.excerpt: This week a new class of "zero trust, zero setup, zero latency" agent sandboxes started trending on GitHub (the nolabs-ai/nono runtime crossed 5,000 stars). The promise is seductive: run untrusted age…
articles.body: This week a new class of "zero trust, zero setup, zero latency" agent sandboxes started trending on GitHub (the nolabs-ai/nono runtime crossed 5,000 stars). The promise is seductive: run untrusted agent code in an isolated runtime and stop worrying about what the model might do. I think that framing is half right. Process isolation solves a real problem by stopping an agent from reading your entire filesystem, but it does not solve the problem that actually bites production agents: an LLM being talked into calling a powerful tool in a way you never intended. Let me explain the gap, then show the code-level pattern I use to close it. 1. What a Sandbox Actually Protects (and What It Doesn't) An agent sandbox is fundamentally an operating-system boundary.

articles.excerpt: Most "computer use" tools take over the machine. The pointer moves, windows jump to the front, and you wait until the agent is done. I wanted an agent to work in one Windows app while I kept typing in…
articles.body: Most "computer use" tools take over the machine. The pointer moves, windows jump to the front, and you wait until the agent is done. I wanted an agent to work in one Windows app while I kept typing in another, so I built Sidehand. What it does Sidehand is an MCP server (plus a CLI and a pi extension) for Windows 10 and 11. Claude, Codex, Cursor or any MCP client can read and operate Windows apps that sit behind the window you are using. It types, clicks, picks from lists and reads the screen as text. Your mouse does not move and your keyboard stays with you. What the agent sees $ sidehand tree "Contoso Orders" window: Contoso Orders (18 elements) e4 Edit "Customer" e12 Button "Submit order" $ sidehand act e4 type "Blue-B Studio" $ sidehand act e12 click One short line per control.

articles.excerpt: If you pay for Claude, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode Go, you have probably been surprised by a rate limit in the middle of a task. I got tired of opening four dashboards to check my pace, so I built BurnB…
articles.body: If you pay for Claude, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode Go, you have probably been surprised by a rate limit in the middle of a task. I got tired of opening four dashboards to check my pace, so I built BurnBar : a small tray app that shows how fast you are using your plans without leaving what you are doing. What it does Four providers: Claude, Codex, OpenCode Go and Cursor, with the session, weekly or monthly windows each one reports, plus reset times. Compact tray popup: click the tray icon for a small usage card anchored beside it. Alerts: milestone cards at 10%, 20% ... 100%, 80% and 95% warnings, reset alerts, snooze and quiet hours. Pace at a glance: progress bars with a pace marker, and a week of history so you can see how you are trending.

articles.title: How to write an AI code review prompt your team will actually read
articles.excerpt: This article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against MergeJudge's public docs. Most AI code review prompts fail the same way. They ask the model to "review this PR thoroughly", the model ob…
articles.body: This article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against MergeJudge's public docs. Most AI code review prompts fail the same way. They ask the model to "review this PR thoroughly", the model obliges with fifteen comments, and within a week the team scrolls past the bot without reading it. The problem is rarely the model. It is the prompt: no repo context, no list of things to skip, no output format and no limit. This post walks through a review prompt you can copy, why each part is there, and how to tell after two weeks whether it is working. The full template lives in our guide: AI code review prompt for pull requests . The five parts of a useful review prompt A prompt that produces comments people act on usually has five parts: A role and a scope.

articles.body: If you're running the official MCP filesystem reference server ( modelcontextprotocol/servers ) on Windows and something's failing in a way that feels like it should just work, there's a real chance it isn't your config. As of November 2026 there are four separate open issues against that server that only reproduce on Windows — and none of them has a merged fix. This is the kind of thing worth checking before you spend an hour reinstalling, re-pathing, or re-reading your client config. Five minutes matching your exact symptom against these four issues will tell you whether you're debugging your own setup or waiting on an upstream fix. The four bugs #5180 — backslash home-path expansion fails. A home-directory path written with native Windows backslashes doesn't expand correctly.

articles.body: AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan.

articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 has traveled further than any other man-made object. | Photo by NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milesto…
articles.body: Voyager 1 has traveled further than any other man-made object. | Photo by NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: the spacecraft is now officially one light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, "very, very far." The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET, and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet - equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours. It's the furthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1's journey isn't over yet. It's been heading towards a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
articles.excerpt: It now takes 24 hours for even a single particle of light to reach Voyager.
articles.body: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.

articles.body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – An… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image captures a piece of the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere.
